newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia products outlook - Imports weighing on market.
newsitem.headline: Asia products outlook - Imports weighing on market.

text.p: An armada of oil tankers filled with gas oil, fuel oil, and naphtha were poised to invade Asia, saending jitters through the market this week, traders said on Monday.
Traders said the imports from North West Europe and the Mediterranean would have difficulty being absorbed by the market at current prices.
"The Chinese have yet to enter the market in a big way since the Lunar New Year holidays (early February) and prices will fall sharply if all the arbitrage cargoes come," one trader said.
Already, there are signs of price pressures, with the gas oil March/April swap spread widening under the weight of the imports.
Sources said about 500,000-tonnes of gas oil were being put together by several traders for shipment to East Asia and India and were most likely to arrive in April.
The March/April swap spread widened to 80 cents on Friday from about 60 cents earlier in the week. By Monday, the spread was almost $1.00.

Traders said the market may be cushioned if a lot of these cargoes ended up in India, but they cautioned that if these were shipped unsold to East Asia, prices in April would weaken, especially if China was still not buying.
At the moment, China was not buying a lot of gas oil as its coastal tanks were full but in land the endusers were facing a shortage and moves were underway to speed up distribution.
Traders said March gas oil would be supported as there was not much prompt gas oil available.
Indonesia was partly supporting demand because of various refinery problems.
Similar scenes were also being played in the fuel oil market but the supply scenario appeared more bearish with ample prompt supplies and more headed towards Asia from the West for April.
Traders said unless China steps in to buy, fuel oil prices might fall below $90.00 per tonne from market assessments of $96.00/$98.00 per tonne on Friday.
Residual fuel stocks in Singapore rose to a nine-month high of 12.299 million tonnes last week, Singapore's Trade Development Board said last Thursday.
On the naphtha market, prices were down 50 cents on Friday on news that 150,000 tonnes of Algerian naphtha was due to arrive in April with a Mexican cargo also offered into the market.

Such arbitrage moves have pressured the East-West spreads to $22-$23 per tonne, down from over $30 last week, a trader said. The arbitrage window has now closed and traders doubted more cargoes would arrive.

Singapore March naphtha swaps were quoted Monday at $22.90/$23.10 per barrel, extending last week's losses, while Japan's open-spec for second-half April was quoted early Monday at $223.00/$224.00 per tonne, from $226.00/$228.00 late last week.
Some traders said prices could fall further, while others said prices should bottom out as the arbitrage cargoes can easily be absorbed by South Korea, Thailand and China. Japan was mostly covered.

State-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corp sold 2.7 million tonnes of full-range naphtha on term between March 1997-February 1998 to buyers in Japan, South Korea and India at a record $13.50 per tonne over Mideast spot quotes on a free-on-board basis.
Traders said the tightness in gasoline extended up to March, with still no sellers were emerging to meet buyers on the Singapore fob market.

Sentiment continued to build on Taiwan's issue of its first half April reformate import tender on Wednesday, just after it awarded its second half March tenders last week, traders said. The tender is due to close March 4, validity until March 6.
